newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan plans T$61.477 bln loans for first homes.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan plans T$61.477 bln loans for first homes.

text.p: Taiwan's interior ministry said on Thursday it was arranging T$61.477 billion in credits from the cabinet's Medium- and Long-term Funds to offer low-cost loans for first-time homebuyers.

"We hope the loan can help reduce first-time homebuyers' interest burden and help solve the oversupply condition in the domestic property market," said Cheng Jung-lung, a deputy director of the interior ministry's construction and planning administration.
The 30-year loan programme, subject to approval by the cabinet's Council on Economic Planning and Development, would bear an annual loan rate of 7.7 percent, Chen told Reuters.
That is equivalent to the one-year postal deposit rate -- currently 6.2 percent -- plus 1.5 percentage points, he said.
The ministry plans to offer the loan in the coming fiscal year starting July 1, 1997, he said.
The Council for Economic Planning and Development oversees the cabinet's huge Medium- and Long-term Funds, which are financed through Taiwan's state postal funds.

To qualify, applicants must be first-time homebuyers as well as low-income nationals, with combined annual family income below T$1.31 million in Taipei, T$1.03 million in Kaohsiung and T$0.83 million in the remaining area of Taiwan, Cheng said.
Modest apartments in urban Taipei sell for about T$8 million (US$291,000). Those in Taipei's suburbs and the regional cities of Taichung and Kaohsiung are around T$5 million (US$182,00).
The proposed loans would be available as a complement to an existing loan project in which qualified applicants can borrow up to T$1.6 million at 5.075 percent, Cheng said.
Under the new proposal, qualified applicants can apply for an additional T$3.4 million at 7.7 percent, he said.
First-time homebuyers using both programmes would be able to borrow up to T$5 million, he said.
Commercial home loans from banks are about 9.0 percent.
The proposal was similar to a 1994-95 central bank scheme that offered some T$100 billion in low-cost loans to first-time homebuyers in a bid to boost the sluggish property market.
The low-income qualifications for the earlier scheme were less stringent than under the new programme.
Cheng said the new scheme was expected to result in the sales of about 20,000 vacant residences.
In 1994, state statisticians estimated there were 820,000 vacant houses in Taiwan, a serious oversupply condition that caused the domestic property to stagnate since a 1989 peak.
No official figures have been released since then.
